46 def _is_int_type(x):
47 """
48 Check if input is of a scalar integer type (so ``5`` and ``array(5)`` will
49 pass, while ``5.0`` and ``array([5])`` will fail.
50 """
51 if np.ndim(x) != 0:
52 # Older versions of NumPy did not raise for np.array([1]).__index__()
53 # This is safe to remove when support for those versions is dropped
54 return False
55 try:
56 operator.index(x)
57 except TypeError:
58 return False
59 else:
60 return True

63 def _real_dtype_for_complex(dtyp, *, xp):
64 if xp.isdtype(dtyp, 'real floating'):
65 return dtyp
66 if dtyp == xp.complex64:
67 return xp.float32
68 elif dtyp == xp.complex128:
69 return xp.float64
70 else:
71 raise ValueError(f"Unknown dtype {dtyp}.")

75 def _logspace(start, stop, num=50, endpoint=True, base=10.0, dtype=None, *, xp):
76 if not isinstance(base, float | int) and xp.asarray(base).ndim > 0:
77 # If base is non-scalar, broadcast it with the others, since it
78 # may influence how axis is interpreted.

80 ndmax = xp.broadcast_arrays(start, stop, base).ndim
81 start, stop, base = (

86 try:
87 result_dt = xp.result_type(start, stop, base)
88 except ValueError:
89 # all of start, stop and base are python scalars
90 result_dt = xp_default_dtype(xp)
91 y = xp.linspace(start, stop, num=num, endpoint=endpoint, dtype=result_dt)
92  
93 yp = xp.pow(base, y)
94 if dtype is None:
95 return yp
96 return xp.astype(yp, dtype, copy=False)

99 def findfreqs(num, den, N, kind='ba'):
100 """
101 Find array of frequencies for computing the response of an analog filter.
102  
103 Parameters
104 ----------
105 num, den : array_like, 1-D
106 The polynomial coefficients of the numerator and denominator of the
107 transfer function of the filter or LTI system, where the coefficients
108 are ordered from highest to lowest degree. Or, the roots of the
109 transfer function numerator and denominator (i.e., zeroes and poles).
110 N : int
111 The length of the array to be computed.
112 kind : str {'ba', 'zp'}, optional
113 Specifies whether the numerator and denominator are specified by their
114 polynomial coefficients ('ba'), or their roots ('zp').
115  
116 Returns
117 -------
118 w : (N,) ndarray
119 A 1-D array of frequencies, logarithmically spaced.
120  
121 Examples
122 --------
123 Find a set of nine frequencies that span the "interesting part" of the
124 frequency response for the filter with the transfer function
125  
126 H(s) = s / (s^2 + 8s + 25)
127  
128 >>> from scipy import signal
129 >>> signal.findfreqs([1, 0], [1, 8, 25], N=9)
130 array([ 1.00000000e-02, 3.16227766e-02, 1.00000000e-01,
131 3.16227766e-01, 1.00000000e+00, 3.16227766e+00,
132 1.00000000e+01, 3.16227766e+01, 1.00000000e+02])
133 """
134 xp = array_namespace(num, den)
135 num, den = map(xp.asarray, (num, den))
136  
137 if kind == 'ba':
138 ep = xpx.atleast_nd(_pu.polyroots(den, xp=xp), ndim=1, xp=xp)
139 tz = xpx.atleast_nd(_pu.polyroots(num, xp=xp), ndim=1, xp=xp)
140 elif kind == 'zp':
141 ep = xpx.atleast_nd(den, ndim=1, xp=xp)
142 tz = xpx.atleast_nd(num, ndim=1, xp=xp)
143 else:
144 raise ValueError("input must be one of {'ba', 'zp'}")
145  
146 ep = xp_float_to_complex(ep, xp=xp)
147 tz = xp_float_to_complex(tz, xp=xp)
148  
149 if ep.shape[0] == 0:
150 ep = xp.asarray([-1000], dtype=ep.dtype)
151  
152 ez = xp.concat((
153 ep[xp.imag(ep) >= 0],
154 tz[(xp.abs(tz) < 1e5) & (xp.imag(tz) >= 0)]
155 ))
156

158 hfreq = xp.round(
159 xp.log10(xp.max(3*xp.abs(xp.real(ez) + integ) + 1.5*xp.imag(ez))) + 0.5
160 )

173 def freqs(b, a, worN=200, plot=None):
174 """
175 Compute frequency response of analog filter.
176  
177 Given the M-order numerator `b` and N-order denominator `a` of an analog
178 filter, compute its frequency response::
179  
180 b[0]*(jw)**M + b[1]*(jw)**(M-1) + ... + b[M]
181 H(w) = ----------------------------------------------
182 a[0]*(jw)**N + a[1]*(jw)**(N-1) + ... + a[N]
183  
184 Parameters
185 ----------
186 b : array_like
187 Numerator of a linear filter.
188 a : array_like
189 Denominator of a linear filter.
190 worN : {None, int, array_like}, optional
191 If None, then compute at 200 frequencies around the interesting parts
192 of the response curve (determined by pole-zero locations). If a single
193 integer, then compute at that many frequencies. Otherwise, compute the
194 response at the angular frequencies (e.g., rad/s) given in `worN`.
195 plot : callable, optional
196 A callable that takes two arguments. If given, the return parameters
197 `w` and `h` are passed to plot. Useful for plotting the frequency
198 response inside `freqs`.
199  
200 Returns
201 -------
202 w : ndarray
203 The angular frequencies at which `h` was computed.
204 h : ndarray
205 The frequency response.
206  
207 See Also
208 --------
209 freqz : Compute the frequency response of a digital filter.
210  
211 Notes
212 -----
213 Using Matplotlib's "plot" function as the callable for `plot` produces
214 unexpected results, this plots the real part of the complex transfer
215 function, not the magnitude. Try ``lambda w, h: plot(w, abs(h))``.
216  
217 Examples
218 --------
219 >>> from scipy.signal import freqs, iirfilter
220 >>> import numpy as np
221  
222 >>> b, a = iirfilter(4, [1, 10], 1, 60, analog=True, ftype='cheby1')
223  
224 >>> w, h = freqs(b, a, worN=np.logspace(-1, 2, 1000))
225  
226 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
227 >>> plt.semilogx(w, 20 * np.log10(abs(h)))
228 >>> plt.xlabel('Frequency [rad/s]')
229 >>> plt.ylabel('Amplitude response [dB]')
230 >>> plt.grid(True)
231 >>> plt.show()
232  
233 """
234 xp = array_namespace(b, a, worN)
235  
236 if worN is None:
237 # For backwards compatibility
238 w = findfreqs(b, a, 200)
239 elif _is_int_type(worN):
240 w = findfreqs(b, a, worN)
241 else:
242 w = xpx.atleast_nd(xp.asarray(worN), ndim=1, xp=xp)
243  
244 s = 1j * w
245 h = _pu.polyval(b, s, xp=xp) / _pu.polyval(a, s, xp=xp)
246 if plot is not None:
247 plot(w, h)
248  
249 return w, h
250

252 def freqs_zpk(z, p, k, worN=200):
253 """
254 Compute frequency response of analog filter.
255  
256 Given the zeros `z`, poles `p`, and gain `k` of a filter, compute its
257 frequency response::
258  
259 (jw-z[0]) * (jw-z[1]) * ... * (jw-z[-1])
260 H(w) = k * ----------------------------------------
261 (jw-p[0]) * (jw-p[1]) * ... * (jw-p[-1])
262  
263 Parameters
264 ----------
265 z : array_like
266 Zeroes of a linear filter
267 p : array_like
268 Poles of a linear filter
269 k : scalar
270 Gain of a linear filter
271 worN : {None, int, array_like}, optional
272 If None, then compute at 200 frequencies around the interesting parts
273 of the response curve (determined by pole-zero locations). If a single
274 integer, then compute at that many frequencies. Otherwise, compute the
275 response at the angular frequencies (e.g., rad/s) given in `worN`.
276  
277 Returns
278 -------
279 w : ndarray
280 The angular frequencies at which `h` was computed.
281 h : ndarray
282 The frequency response.
283  
284 See Also
285 --------
286 freqs : Compute the frequency response of an analog filter in TF form
287 freqz : Compute the frequency response of a digital filter in TF form
288 freqz_zpk : Compute the frequency response of a digital filter in ZPK form
289  
290 Notes
291 -----
292 .. versionadded:: 0.19.0
293  
294 Examples
295 --------
296 >>> import numpy as np
297 >>> from scipy.signal import freqs_zpk, iirfilter
298  
299 >>> z, p, k = iirfilter(4, [1, 10], 1, 60, analog=True, ftype='cheby1',
300 ... output='zpk')
301  
302 >>> w, h = freqs_zpk(z, p, k, worN=np.logspace(-1, 2, 1000))
303  
304 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
305 >>> plt.semilogx(w, 20 * np.log10(abs(h)))
306 >>> plt.xlabel('Frequency [rad/s]')
307 >>> plt.ylabel('Amplitude response [dB]')
308 >>> plt.grid(True)
309 >>> plt.show()
310  
311 """
312 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
313 z, p = map(xp.asarray, (z, p))
314  
  • E501 Line too long (82 > 79 characters)
315 # NB: k is documented to be a scalar; for backwards compat we keep allowing it
  • E501 Line too long (80 > 79 characters)
316 # to be a size-1 array, but it does not influence the namespace calculation.
317 k = xp.asarray(k, dtype=xp_default_dtype(xp))
318 if xp_size(k) > 1:
319 raise ValueError('k must be a single scalar gain')
320  
321 if worN is None:
322 # For backwards compatibility
323 w = findfreqs(z, p, 200, kind='zp')

326 else:

330 s = 1j * w

332 den = _pu.npp_polyvalfromroots(s, p, xp=xp)
333 h = k * num/den
334 return w, h

337 def freqz(b, a=1, worN=512, whole=False, plot=None, fs=2*pi,
338 include_nyquist=False):
339 """
340 Compute the frequency response of a digital filter.
341  
342 Given the M-order numerator `b` and N-order denominator `a` of a digital
343 filter, compute its frequency response::
344  
345 jw -jw -jwM
346 jw B(e ) b[0] + b[1]e + ... + b[M]e
347 H(e ) = ------ = -----------------------------------
348 jw -jw -jwN
349 A(e ) a[0] + a[1]e + ... + a[N]e
350  
351 Parameters
352 ----------
353 b : array_like
354 Numerator of a linear filter. If `b` has dimension greater than 1,
355 it is assumed that the coefficients are stored in the first dimension,
356 and ``b.shape[1:]``, ``a.shape[1:]``, and the shape of the frequencies
357 array must be compatible for broadcasting.
358 a : array_like
359 Denominator of a linear filter. If `b` has dimension greater than 1,
360 it is assumed that the coefficients are stored in the first dimension,
361 and ``b.shape[1:]``, ``a.shape[1:]``, and the shape of the frequencies
362 array must be compatible for broadcasting.
363 worN : {None, int, array_like}, optional
364 If a single integer, then compute at that many frequencies (default is
365 N=512). This is a convenient alternative to::
366  
367 np.linspace(0, fs if whole else fs/2, N, endpoint=include_nyquist)
368  
369 Using a number that is fast for FFT computations can result in
370 faster computations (see Notes).
371  
372 If an array_like, compute the response at the frequencies given.
373 These are in the same units as `fs`.
374 whole : bool, optional
375 Normally, frequencies are computed from 0 to the Nyquist frequency,
376 fs/2 (upper-half of unit-circle). If `whole` is True, compute
377 frequencies from 0 to fs. Ignored if worN is array_like.
378 plot : callable
379 A callable that takes two arguments. If given, the return parameters
380 `w` and `h` are passed to plot. Useful for plotting the frequency
381 response inside `freqz`.
382 fs : float, optional
383 The sampling frequency of the digital system. Defaults to 2*pi
384 radians/sample (so w is from 0 to pi).
385  
386 .. versionadded:: 1.2.0
387 include_nyquist : bool, optional
388 If `whole` is False and `worN` is an integer, setting `include_nyquist`
389 to True will include the last frequency (Nyquist frequency) and is
390 otherwise ignored.
391  
392 .. versionadded:: 1.5.0
393  
394 Returns
395 -------
396 w : ndarray
397 The frequencies at which `h` was computed, in the same units as `fs`.
398 By default, `w` is normalized to the range [0, pi) (radians/sample).
399 h : ndarray
400 The frequency response, as complex numbers.
401  
402 See Also
403 --------
404 freqz_zpk
405 freqz_sos
406  
407 Notes
408 -----
409 Using Matplotlib's :func:`matplotlib.pyplot.plot` function as the callable
410 for `plot` produces unexpected results, as this plots the real part of the
411 complex transfer function, not the magnitude.
412 Try ``lambda w, h: plot(w, np.abs(h))``.
413  
414 A direct computation via (R)FFT is used to compute the frequency response
415 when the following conditions are met:
416  
417 1. An integer value is given for `worN`.
418 2. `worN` is fast to compute via FFT (i.e.,
419 `next_fast_len(worN) <scipy.fft.next_fast_len>` equals `worN`).
420 3. The denominator coefficients are a single value (``a.shape[0] == 1``).
421 4. `worN` is at least as long as the numerator coefficients
422 (``worN >= b.shape[0]``).
423 5. If ``b.ndim > 1``, then ``b.shape[-1] == 1``.
424  
425 For long FIR filters, the FFT approach can have lower error and be much
426 faster than the equivalent direct polynomial calculation.
427  
428 Examples
429 --------
430 >>> from scipy import signal
431 >>> import numpy as np
432 >>> taps, f_c = 80, 1.0 # number of taps and cut-off frequency
433 >>> b = signal.firwin(taps, f_c, window=('kaiser', 8), fs=2*np.pi)
434 >>> w, h = signal.freqz(b)
435  
436 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
437 >>> fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(tight_layout=True)
438 >>> ax1.set_title(f"Frequency Response of {taps} tap FIR Filter" +
439 ... f"($f_c={f_c}$ rad/sample)")
440 >>> ax1.axvline(f_c, color='black', linestyle=':', linewidth=0.8)
441 >>> ax1.plot(w, 20 * np.log10(abs(h)), 'C0')
442 >>> ax1.set_ylabel("Amplitude in dB", color='C0')
443 >>> ax1.set(xlabel="Frequency in rad/sample", xlim=(0, np.pi))
444  
445 >>> ax2 = ax1.twinx()
446 >>> phase = np.unwrap(np.angle(h))
447 >>> ax2.plot(w, phase, 'C1')
448 >>> ax2.set_ylabel('Phase [rad]', color='C1')
449 >>> ax2.grid(True)
450 >>> ax2.axis('tight')
451 >>> plt.show()
452  
453 Broadcasting Examples
454  
455 Suppose we have two FIR filters whose coefficients are stored in the
456 rows of an array with shape (2, 25). For this demonstration, we'll
457 use random data:
458  
459 >>> rng = np.random.default_rng()
460 >>> b = rng.random((2, 25))
461  
462 To compute the frequency response for these two filters with one call
463 to `freqz`, we must pass in ``b.T``, because `freqz` expects the first
464 axis to hold the coefficients. We must then extend the shape with a
465 trivial dimension of length 1 to allow broadcasting with the array
466 of frequencies. That is, we pass in ``b.T[..., np.newaxis]``, which has
467 shape (25, 2, 1):
468  
469 >>> w, h = signal.freqz(b.T[..., np.newaxis], worN=1024)
470 >>> w.shape
471 (1024,)
472 >>> h.shape
473 (2, 1024)
474  
475 Now, suppose we have two transfer functions, with the same numerator
476 coefficients ``b = [0.5, 0.5]``. The coefficients for the two denominators
477 are stored in the first dimension of the 2-D array `a`::
478  
479 a = [ 1 1 ]
480 [ -0.25, -0.5 ]
481  
482 >>> b = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
483 >>> a = np.array([[1, 1], [-0.25, -0.5]])
484  
485 Only `a` is more than 1-D. To make it compatible for
486 broadcasting with the frequencies, we extend it with a trivial dimension
487 in the call to `freqz`:
488  
489 >>> w, h = signal.freqz(b, a[..., np.newaxis], worN=1024)
490 >>> w.shape
491 (1024,)
492 >>> h.shape
493 (2, 1024)
494  
495 """
496 xp = array_namespace(b, a)
497

575 def freqz_zpk(z, p, k, worN=512, whole=False, fs=2*pi):
576 r"""
577 Compute the frequency response of a digital filter in ZPK form.
578  
579 Given the Zeros, Poles and Gain of a digital filter, compute its frequency
580 response:
581  
582 :math:`H(z)=k \prod_i (z - Z[i]) / \prod_j (z - P[j])`
583  
584 where :math:`k` is the `gain`, :math:`Z` are the `zeros` and :math:`P` are
585 the `poles`.
586  
587 Parameters
588 ----------
589 z : array_like
590 Zeroes of a linear filter
591 p : array_like
592 Poles of a linear filter
593 k : scalar
594 Gain of a linear filter
595 worN : {None, int, array_like}, optional
596 If a single integer, then compute at that many frequencies (default is
597 N=512).
598  
599 If an array_like, compute the response at the frequencies given.
600 These are in the same units as `fs`.
601 whole : bool, optional
602 Normally, frequencies are computed from 0 to the Nyquist frequency,
603 fs/2 (upper-half of unit-circle). If `whole` is True, compute
604 frequencies from 0 to fs. Ignored if w is array_like.
605 fs : float, optional
606 The sampling frequency of the digital system. Defaults to 2*pi
607 radians/sample (so w is from 0 to pi).
608  
609 .. versionadded:: 1.2.0
610  
611 Returns
612 -------
613 w : ndarray
614 The frequencies at which `h` was computed, in the same units as `fs`.
615 By default, `w` is normalized to the range [0, pi) (radians/sample).
616 h : ndarray
617 The frequency response, as complex numbers.
618  
619 See Also

694 def group_delay(system, w=512, whole=False, fs=2*pi):
695 r"""Compute the group delay of a digital filter.
696  
697 The group delay measures by how many samples amplitude envelopes of
698 various spectral components of a signal are delayed by a filter.
699 It is formally defined as the derivative of continuous (unwrapped) phase::
700  
701 d jw
702 D(w) = - -- arg H(e)
703 dw
704  
705 Parameters
706 ----------
707 system : tuple of array_like (b, a)
708 Numerator and denominator coefficients of a filter transfer function.
709 w : {None, int, array_like}, optional
710 If a single integer, then compute at that many frequencies (default is
711 N=512).
712  
713 If an array_like, compute the delay at the frequencies given. These
714 are in the same units as `fs`.
715 whole : bool, optional
716 Normally, frequencies are computed from 0 to the Nyquist frequency,
717 fs/2 (upper-half of unit-circle). If `whole` is True, compute
718 frequencies from 0 to fs. Ignored if w is array_like.
719 fs : float, optional
720 The sampling frequency of the digital system. Defaults to 2*pi
721 radians/sample (so w is from 0 to pi).
722  
723 .. versionadded:: 1.2.0
724  
725 Returns
726 -------
727 w : ndarray
728 The frequencies at which group delay was computed, in the same units
729 as `fs`. By default, `w` is normalized to the range [0, pi)
730 (radians/sample).
731 gd : ndarray
732 The group delay.
733  
734 See Also
735 --------
736 freqz : Frequency response of a digital filter
737  
738 Notes
739 -----
740 The similar function in MATLAB is called `grpdelay`.
741  
742 If the transfer function :math:`H(z)` has zeros or poles on the unit
743 circle, the group delay at corresponding frequencies is undefined.
744 When such a case arises the warning is raised and the group delay
745 is set to 0 at those frequencies.
746  
  • E501 Line too long (86 > 79 characters)
747 For the details of numerical computation of the group delay refer to [1]_ or [2]_.
748  
749 .. versionadded:: 0.16.0
750  
751 References
752 ----------
753 .. [1] Richard G. Lyons, "Understanding Digital Signal Processing,
754 3rd edition", p. 830.
755 .. [2] Julius O. Smith III, "Numerical Computation of Group Delay",
756 in "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications",
757 online book, 2007,
758 https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/fp/Numerical_Computation_Group_Delay.html
759  
760 Examples
761 --------
762 >>> from scipy import signal
763 >>> b, a = signal.iirdesign(0.1, 0.3, 5, 50, ftype='cheby1')
764 >>> w, gd = signal.group_delay((b, a))
765  
766 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
767 >>> plt.title('Digital filter group delay')
768 >>> plt.plot(w, gd)
769 >>> plt.ylabel('Group delay [samples]')
770 >>> plt.xlabel('Frequency [rad/sample]')
771 >>> plt.show()
772  
773 """
774 if w is None:
775 # For backwards compatibility
776 w = 512
777  
778 fs = _validate_fs(fs, allow_none=False)
779  
780 if _is_int_type(w):
781 if whole:
782 w = np.linspace(0, 2 * pi, w, endpoint=False)
783 else:
784 w = np.linspace(0, pi, w, endpoint=False)
785 else:
786 w = np.atleast_1d(w)
787 w = 2*pi*w/fs
788  
789 b, a = map(np.atleast_1d, system)
790 c = np.convolve(b, conjugate(a[::-1]))
791 cr = c * np.arange(c.size)
792 z = np.exp(-1j * w)
793 num = np.polyval(cr[::-1], z)
794 den = np.polyval(c[::-1], z)
795 gd = np.real(num / den) - a.size + 1
796 singular = ~np.isfinite(gd)
797 near_singular = np.absolute(den) < 10 * EPSILON
798  
799 if np.any(singular):
800 gd[singular] = 0
801 warnings.warn(
802 "The group delay is singular at frequencies "
803 f"[{', '.join(f'{ws:.3f}' for ws in w[singular])}], setting to 0",
804 stacklevel=2
805 )
806  
807 elif np.any(near_singular):
808 warnings.warn(
809 "The filter's denominator is extremely small at frequencies "
810 f"[{', '.join(f'{ws:.3f}' for ws in w[near_singular])}], "
811 "around which a singularity may be present",
812 stacklevel=2
813 )
814  
815 w = w*(fs/(2*pi))
816  
817 return w, gd

820 def _validate_sos(sos, xp=None):
821 """Helper to validate a SOS input"""
822 if xp is None:
823 xp = np # backcompat, cf sosfilt, sosfiltfilt

832 if not xp.all(sos[:, 3] == 1):

834 return sos, n_sections

837 def freqz_sos(sos, worN=512, whole=False, fs=2*pi):
838 r"""
839 Compute the frequency response of a digital filter in SOS format.
840  
841 Given `sos`, an array with shape (n, 6) of second order sections of
842 a digital filter, compute the frequency response of the system function::
843  
844 B0(z) B1(z) B{n-1}(z)
845 H(z) = ----- * ----- * ... * ---------
846 A0(z) A1(z) A{n-1}(z)
847  
848 for z = exp(omega*1j), where B{k}(z) and A{k}(z) are numerator and
849 denominator of the transfer function of the k-th second order section.
850  
851 Parameters
852 ----------
853 sos : array_like
854 Array of second-order filter coefficients, must have shape
855 ``(n_sections, 6)``. Each row corresponds to a second-order
856 section, with the first three columns providing the numerator
857 coefficients and the last three providing the denominator
858 coefficients.
859 worN : {None, int, array_like}, optional
860 If a single integer, then compute at that many frequencies (default is
861 N=512). Using a number that is fast for FFT computations can result
862 in faster computations (see Notes of `freqz`).
863  
864 If an array_like, compute the response at the frequencies given (must
865 be 1-D). These are in the same units as `fs`.
866 whole : bool, optional
867 Normally, frequencies are computed from 0 to the Nyquist frequency,
868 fs/2 (upper-half of unit-circle). If `whole` is True, compute
869 frequencies from 0 to fs.
870 fs : float, optional
871 The sampling frequency of the digital system. Defaults to 2*pi
872 radians/sample (so w is from 0 to pi).
873  
874 .. versionadded:: 1.2.0
875  
876 Returns
877 -------
878 w : ndarray
879 The frequencies at which `h` was computed, in the same units as `fs`.
880 By default, `w` is normalized to the range [0, pi) (radians/sample).
881 h : ndarray
882 The frequency response, as complex numbers.
883  
884 See Also
885 --------
886 freqz, sosfilt, sosfreqz
887  
888 Notes
889 -----
890 This function used to be called ``sosfreqz`` in older versions (≥ 0.19.0)
  • W293 Blank line contains whitespace
891
892 .. versionadded:: 1.15.0
  • W293 Blank line contains whitespace
893
894 Examples
895 --------
896 Design a 15th-order bandpass filter in SOS format.
897  
898 >>> from scipy import signal
899 >>> import numpy as np
900 >>> sos = signal.ellip(15, 0.5, 60, (0.2, 0.4), btype='bandpass',
901 ... output='sos')
902  
903 Compute the frequency response at 1500 points from DC to Nyquist.
904  
905 >>> w, h = signal.freqz_sos(sos, worN=1500)
906  
907 Plot the response.
908  
909 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
910 >>> plt.subplot(2, 1, 1)
911 >>> db = 20*np.log10(np.maximum(np.abs(h), 1e-5))
912 >>> plt.plot(w/np.pi, db)
913 >>> plt.ylim(-75, 5)
914 >>> plt.grid(True)
915 >>> plt.yticks([0, -20, -40, -60])
916 >>> plt.ylabel('Gain [dB]')
917 >>> plt.title('Frequency Response')
918 >>> plt.subplot(2, 1, 2)
919 >>> plt.plot(w/np.pi, np.angle(h))
920 >>> plt.grid(True)
921 >>> plt.yticks([-np.pi, -0.5*np.pi, 0, 0.5*np.pi, np.pi],
922 ... [r'$-\pi$', r'$-\pi/2$', '0', r'$\pi/2$', r'$\pi$'])
923 >>> plt.ylabel('Phase [rad]')
924 >>> plt.xlabel('Normalized frequency (1.0 = Nyquist)')
925 >>> plt.show()
926  
927 If the same filter is implemented as a single transfer function,
928 numerical error corrupts the frequency response:
929  
930 >>> b, a = signal.ellip(15, 0.5, 60, (0.2, 0.4), btype='bandpass',
931 ... output='ba')
932 >>> w, h = signal.freqz(b, a, worN=1500)
933 >>> plt.subplot(2, 1, 1)
934 >>> db = 20*np.log10(np.maximum(np.abs(h), 1e-5))
935 >>> plt.plot(w/np.pi, db)
936 >>> plt.ylim(-75, 5)
937 >>> plt.grid(True)
938 >>> plt.yticks([0, -20, -40, -60])
939 >>> plt.ylabel('Gain [dB]')
940 >>> plt.title('Frequency Response')
941 >>> plt.subplot(2, 1, 2)
942 >>> plt.plot(w/np.pi, np.angle(h))
943 >>> plt.grid(True)
944 >>> plt.yticks([-np.pi, -0.5*np.pi, 0, 0.5*np.pi, np.pi],
945 ... [r'$-\pi$', r'$-\pi/2$', '0', r'$\pi/2$', r'$\pi$'])
946 >>> plt.ylabel('Phase [rad]')
947 >>> plt.xlabel('Normalized frequency (1.0 = Nyquist)')
948 >>> plt.show()
949  
950 """
951 xp = array_namespace(sos)
952  
953 fs = _validate_fs(fs, allow_none=False)
954  
955 sos, n_sections = _validate_sos(sos, xp)
956 if n_sections == 0:
957 raise ValueError('Cannot compute frequencies with no sections')
958 h = 1.
959 for j in range(sos.shape[0]):
960 row = sos[j, :]
961 w, rowh = freqz(row[:3], row[3:], worN=worN, whole=whole, fs=fs)
962 h *= rowh
963 return w, h

980 def _cplxreal(z, tol=None):
981 """
982 Split into complex and real parts, combining conjugate pairs.
983  
  • E501 Line too long (80 > 79 characters)
984 The 1-D input vector `z` is split up into its complex (`zc`) and real (`zr`)
985 elements. Every complex element must be part of a complex-conjugate pair,
986 which are combined into a single number (with positive imaginary part) in
987 the output. Two complex numbers are considered a conjugate pair if their
988 real and imaginary parts differ in magnitude by less than ``tol * abs(z)``.
989  
990 Parameters
991 ----------
992 z : array_like
993 Vector of complex numbers to be sorted and split
994 tol : float, optional
995 Relative tolerance for testing realness and conjugate equality.
996 Default is ``100 * spacing(1)`` of `z`'s data type (i.e., 2e-14 for
997 float64)
998  
999 Returns
1000 -------
1001 zc : ndarray
1002 Complex elements of `z`, with each pair represented by a single value
1003 having positive imaginary part, sorted first by real part, and then
1004 by magnitude of imaginary part. The pairs are averaged when combined
1005 to reduce error.
1006 zr : ndarray
1007 Real elements of `z` (those having imaginary part less than
1008 `tol` times their magnitude), sorted by value.
1009  
1010 Raises
1011 ------
1012 ValueError
1013 If there are any complex numbers in `z` for which a conjugate
1014 cannot be found.
1015  
1016 See Also
1017 --------
1018 _cplxpair
1019  
1020 Examples
1021 --------
1022 >>> from scipy.signal._filter_design import _cplxreal
1023 >>> a = [4, 3, 1, 2-2j, 2+2j, 2-1j, 2+1j, 2-1j, 2+1j, 1+1j, 1-1j]
1024 >>> zc, zr = _cplxreal(a)
1025 >>> print(zc)
1026 [ 1.+1.j 2.+1.j 2.+1.j 2.+2.j]
1027 >>> print(zr)
1028 [ 1. 3. 4.]
1029 """
1030  
1031 z = atleast_1d(z)
1032 if z.size == 0:
1033 return z, z
1034 elif z.ndim != 1:
1035 raise ValueError('_cplxreal only accepts 1-D input')
1036  
1037 if tol is None:
1038 # Get tolerance from dtype of input
1039 tol = 100 * np.finfo((1.0 * z).dtype).eps
1040  
1041 # Sort by real part, magnitude of imaginary part (speed up further sorting)
1042 z = z[np.lexsort((abs(z.imag), z.real))]
1043  
1044 # Split reals from conjugate pairs
1045 real_indices = abs(z.imag) <= tol * abs(z)
1046 zr = z[real_indices].real
1047  
1048 if len(zr) == len(z):
1049 # Input is entirely real
1050 return array([]), zr
1051  
1052 # Split positive and negative halves of conjugates
1053 z = z[~real_indices]
1054 zp = z[z.imag > 0]
1055 zn = z[z.imag < 0]
1056  
1057 if len(zp) != len(zn):
1058 raise ValueError('Array contains complex value with no matching '
1059 'conjugate.')
1060  
1061 # Find runs of (approximately) the same real part
1062 same_real = np.diff(zp.real) <= tol * abs(zp[:-1])
1063 diffs = np.diff(concatenate(([0], same_real, [0])))
1064 run_starts = np.nonzero(diffs > 0)[0]
1065 run_stops = np.nonzero(diffs < 0)[0]
1066  
1067 # Sort each run by their imaginary parts
1068 for i in range(len(run_starts)):
1069 start = run_starts[i]
1070 stop = run_stops[i] + 1
1071 for chunk in (zp[start:stop], zn[start:stop]):
1072 chunk[...] = chunk[np.lexsort([abs(chunk.imag)])]
1073  
1074 # Check that negatives match positives
1075 if any(abs(zp - zn.conj()) > tol * abs(zn)):
1076 raise ValueError('Array contains complex value with no matching '
1077 'conjugate.')
1078  
1079 # Average out numerical inaccuracy in real vs imag parts of pairs
1080 zc = (zp + zn.conj()) / 2
1081  
1082 return zc, zr
1083  
1084  
1085 def _cplxpair(z, tol=None):
1086 """
1087 Sort into pairs of complex conjugates.
1088  
1089 Complex conjugates in `z` are sorted by increasing real part. In each
1090 pair, the number with negative imaginary part appears first.
1091  
1092 If pairs have identical real parts, they are sorted by increasing
1093 imaginary magnitude.
1094  
1095 Two complex numbers are considered a conjugate pair if their real and
1096 imaginary parts differ in magnitude by less than ``tol * abs(z)``. The
1097 pairs are forced to be exact complex conjugates by averaging the positive
1098 and negative values.
1099  
1100 Purely real numbers are also sorted, but placed after the complex
1101 conjugate pairs. A number is considered real if its imaginary part is
1102 smaller than `tol` times the magnitude of the number.
1103  
1104 Parameters
1105 ----------
1106 z : array_like
1107 1-D input array to be sorted.
1108 tol : float, optional
1109 Relative tolerance for testing realness and conjugate equality.
1110 Default is ``100 * spacing(1)`` of `z`'s data type (i.e., 2e-14 for
1111 float64)
1112  
1113 Returns
1114 -------
1115 y : ndarray
1116 Complex conjugate pairs followed by real numbers.
1117  
1118 Raises
1119 ------
1120 ValueError
1121 If there are any complex numbers in `z` for which a conjugate
1122 cannot be found.
1123  
1124 See Also
1125 --------
1126 _cplxreal
1127  
1128 Examples
1129 --------
1130 >>> from scipy.signal._filter_design import _cplxpair
1131 >>> a = [4, 3, 1, 2-2j, 2+2j, 2-1j, 2+1j, 2-1j, 2+1j, 1+1j, 1-1j]
1132 >>> z = _cplxpair(a)
1133 >>> print(z)
1134 [ 1.-1.j 1.+1.j 2.-1.j 2.+1.j 2.-1.j 2.+1.j 2.-2.j 2.+2.j 1.+0.j
1135 3.+0.j 4.+0.j]
1136 """
1137  
1138 z = atleast_1d(z)
1139 if z.size == 0 or np.isrealobj(z):
1140 return np.sort(z)
1141  
1142 if z.ndim != 1:
1143 raise ValueError('z must be 1-D')
1144  
1145 zc, zr = _cplxreal(z, tol)
1146  
1147 # Interleave complex values and their conjugates, with negative imaginary
1148 # parts first in each pair
1149 zc = np.dstack((zc.conj(), zc)).flatten()
1150 z = np.append(zc, zr)
1151 return z
1152  
1153  
1154 def tf2zpk(b, a):
1155 r"""Return zero, pole, gain (z, p, k) representation from a numerator,
1156 denominator representation of a linear filter.
1157  
1158 Parameters
1159 ----------
1160 b : array_like
1161 Numerator polynomial coefficients.
1162 a : array_like
1163 Denominator polynomial coefficients.
1164  
1165 Returns
1166 -------
1167 z : ndarray
1168 Zeros of the transfer function.
1169 p : ndarray
1170 Poles of the transfer function.
1171 k : float
1172 System gain.
1173  
1174 Notes
1175 -----
1176 If some values of `b` are too close to 0, they are removed. In that case,
1177 a BadCoefficients warning is emitted.
1178  
1179 The `b` and `a` arrays are interpreted as coefficients for positive,
1180 descending powers of the transfer function variable. So the inputs
1181 :math:`b = [b_0, b_1, ..., b_M]` and :math:`a =[a_0, a_1, ..., a_N]`
1182 can represent an analog filter of the form:
1183  
1184 .. math::
1185  
1186 H(s) = \frac
1187 {b_0 s^M + b_1 s^{(M-1)} + \cdots + b_M}
1188 {a_0 s^N + a_1 s^{(N-1)} + \cdots + a_N}
1189  
1190 or a discrete-time filter of the form:
1191  
1192 .. math::
1193  
1194 H(z) = \frac
1195 {b_0 z^M + b_1 z^{(M-1)} + \cdots + b_M}
1196 {a_0 z^N + a_1 z^{(N-1)} + \cdots + a_N}
1197  
1198 This "positive powers" form is found more commonly in controls
1199 engineering. If `M` and `N` are equal (which is true for all filters
1200 generated by the bilinear transform), then this happens to be equivalent
1201 to the "negative powers" discrete-time form preferred in DSP:
1202  
1203 .. math::
1204  
1205 H(z) = \frac
1206 {b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + \cdots + b_M z^{-M}}
1207 {a_0 + a_1 z^{-1} + \cdots + a_N z^{-N}}
1208  
1209 Although this is true for common filters, remember that this is not true
1210 in the general case. If `M` and `N` are not equal, the discrete-time
1211 transfer function coefficients must first be converted to the "positive
1212 powers" form before finding the poles and zeros.
1213  
1214 Examples
1215 --------
1216 Find the zeroes, poles and gain of
1217 a filter with the transfer function
1218  
1219 .. math::
1220  
1221 H(s) = \frac{3s^2}{s^2 + 5s + 13}
1222  
1223 >>> from scipy.signal import tf2zpk
1224 >>> tf2zpk([3, 0, 0], [1, 5, 13])
1225 ( array([ 0. , 0. ]),
1226 array([ -2.5+2.59807621j , -2.5-2.59807621j]),
1227 3.0)
1228 """
1229 xp = array_namespace(b, a)
1230 b, a = normalize(b, a)
1231  
1232 a, b = xp_promote(a, b, xp=xp, force_floating=True)
1233  
1234 k = b[0]
1235 b = b / b[0]
1236 z = _pu.polyroots(b, xp=xp)
1237 p = _pu.polyroots(a, xp=xp)
1238 return z, p, k
1239  
1240  
1241 def zpk2tf(z, p, k):
1242 r"""
1243 Return polynomial transfer function representation from zeros and poles
1244  
1245 Parameters
1246 ----------
1247 z : array_like
1248 Zeros of the transfer function.
1249 p : array_like
1250 Poles of the transfer function.
1251 k : float
1252 System gain.
1253  
1254 Returns
1255 -------
1256 b : ndarray
1257 Numerator polynomial coefficients.
1258 a : ndarray
1259 Denominator polynomial coefficients.
1260  
1261 Examples
1262 --------
1263 Find the polynomial representation of a transfer function H(s)
1264 using its 'zpk' (Zero-Pole-Gain) representation.
1265  
1266 .. math::
1267  
1268 H(z) = 5 \frac
1269 { (s - 2)(s - 6) }
1270 { (s - 1)(s - 8) }
1271  
1272 >>> from scipy.signal import zpk2tf
1273 >>> z = [2, 6]
1274 >>> p = [1, 8]
1275 >>> k = 5
1276 >>> zpk2tf(z, p, k)
1277 ( array([ 5., -40., 60.]), array([ 1., -9., 8.]))
1278 """
1279 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
1280 z, p, k = map(xp.asarray, (z, p, k))
1281  
1282 z = xpx.atleast_nd(z, ndim=1, xp=xp)
1283 k = xpx.atleast_nd(k, ndim=1, xp=xp)
1284 if xp.isdtype(k.dtype, 'integral'):
1285 k = xp.astype(k, xp_default_dtype(xp))
1286  
1287 if z.ndim > 1:
1288 temp = _pu.poly(z[0], xp=xp)
1289 b = xp.empty((z.shape[0], z.shape[1] + 1), dtype=temp.dtype)
1290 if k.shape[0] == 1:
1291 k = [k[0]] * z.shape[0]
1292 for i in range(z.shape[0]):
1293 b[i] = k[i] * _pu.poly(z[i], xp=xp)
1294 else:
1295 b = k * _pu.poly(z, xp=xp)
1296  
1297 a = _pu.poly(p, xp=xp)
1298 a = xpx.atleast_nd(xp.asarray(a), ndim=1, xp=xp)
1299  
1300 return b, a
1301

1303 def tf2sos(b, a, pairing=None, *, analog=False):
1304 r"""
1305 Return second-order sections from transfer function representation
1306  
1307 Parameters
1308 ----------
1309 b : array_like
1310 Numerator polynomial coefficients.
1311 a : array_like
1312 Denominator polynomial coefficients.
1313 pairing : {None, 'nearest', 'keep_odd', 'minimal'}, optional
1314 The method to use to combine pairs of poles and zeros into sections.
1315 See `zpk2sos` for information and restrictions on `pairing` and
1316 `analog` arguments.
1317 analog : bool, optional
1318 If True, system is analog, otherwise discrete.
1319  
1320 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
1321  
1322 Returns
1323 -------
1324 sos : ndarray
1325 Array of second-order filter coefficients, with shape
1326 ``(n_sections, 6)``. See `sosfilt` for the SOS filter format
1327 specification.
1328  
1329 See Also
1330 --------
1331 zpk2sos, sosfilt
1332  
1333 Notes
1334 -----
1335 It is generally discouraged to convert from TF to SOS format, since doing
1336 so usually will not improve numerical precision errors. Instead, consider
1337 designing filters in ZPK format and converting directly to SOS. TF is
1338 converted to SOS by first converting to ZPK format, then converting
1339 ZPK to SOS.
1340  
1341 .. versionadded:: 0.16.0
1342  
1343 Examples
1344 --------
1345 Find the 'sos' (second-order sections) of the transfer function H(s)
1346 using its polynomial representation.
1347  
1348 .. math::
1349  
1350 H(s) = \frac{s^2 - 3.5s - 2}{s^4 + 3s^3 - 15s^2 - 19s + 30}
1351  
1352 >>> from scipy.signal import tf2sos
1353 >>> tf2sos([1, -3.5, -2], [1, 3, -15, -19, 30], analog=True)
1354 array([[ 0. , 0. , 1. , 1. , 2. , -15. ],
1355 [ 1. , -3.5, -2. , 1. , 1. , -2. ]])
1356 """
1357 return zpk2sos(*tf2zpk(b, a), pairing=pairing, analog=analog)

1453 def _nearest_real_complex_idx(fro, to, which):
1454 """Get the next closest real or complex element based on distance"""
1455 assert which in ('real', 'complex', 'any')
1456 order = np.argsort(np.abs(fro - to))
1457 if which == 'any':
1458 return order[0]
1459 else:
1460 mask = np.isreal(fro[order])
1461 if which == 'complex':
1462 mask = ~mask
1463 return order[np.nonzero(mask)[0][0]]

1466 def _single_zpksos(z, p, k):

1469 b, a = zpk2tf(z, p, k)
1470 sos[3-len(b):3] = b
1471 sos[6-len(a):6] = a
1472 return sos

1475 def zpk2sos(z, p, k, pairing=None, *, analog=False):
1476 """Return second-order sections from zeros, poles, and gain of a system
1477  
1478 Parameters
1479 ----------
1480 z : array_like
1481 Zeros of the transfer function.
1482 p : array_like
1483 Poles of the transfer function.
1484 k : float
1485 System gain.
1486 pairing : {None, 'nearest', 'keep_odd', 'minimal'}, optional
1487 The method to use to combine pairs of poles and zeros into sections.
1488 If analog is False and pairing is None, pairing is set to 'nearest';
1489 if analog is True, pairing must be 'minimal', and is set to that if
1490 it is None.
1491 analog : bool, optional
1492 If True, system is analog, otherwise discrete.
1493  
1494 .. versionadded:: 1.8.0
1495  
1496 Returns
1497 -------
1498 sos : ndarray
1499 Array of second-order filter coefficients, with shape
1500 ``(n_sections, 6)``. See `sosfilt` for the SOS filter format
1501 specification.
1502  
1503 See Also
1504 --------
1505 sosfilt
1506  
1507 Notes
1508 -----
1509 The algorithm used to convert ZPK to SOS format is designed to
1510 minimize errors due to numerical precision issues. The pairing
1511 algorithm attempts to minimize the peak gain of each biquadratic
1512 section. This is done by pairing poles with the nearest zeros, starting
1513 with the poles closest to the unit circle for discrete-time systems, and
1514 poles closest to the imaginary axis for continuous-time systems.
1515  
1516 ``pairing='minimal'`` outputs may not be suitable for `sosfilt`,
1517 and ``analog=True`` outputs will never be suitable for `sosfilt`.
1518  
1519 *Algorithms*
1520  
1521 The steps in the ``pairing='nearest'``, ``pairing='keep_odd'``,
1522 and ``pairing='minimal'`` algorithms are mostly shared. The
1523 ``'nearest'`` algorithm attempts to minimize the peak gain, while
1524 ``'keep_odd'`` minimizes peak gain under the constraint that
1525 odd-order systems should retain one section as first order.
1526 ``'minimal'`` is similar to ``'keep_odd'``, but no additional
1527 poles or zeros are introduced
1528  
1529 The algorithm steps are as follows:
1530  
1531 As a pre-processing step for ``pairing='nearest'``,
1532 ``pairing='keep_odd'``, add poles or zeros to the origin as
1533 necessary to obtain the same number of poles and zeros for
1534 pairing. If ``pairing == 'nearest'`` and there are an odd number
1535 of poles, add an additional pole and a zero at the origin.
1536  
1537 The following steps are then iterated over until no more poles or
1538 zeros remain:
1539  
1540 1. Take the (next remaining) pole (complex or real) closest to the
1541 unit circle (or imaginary axis, for ``analog=True``) to
1542 begin a new filter section.
1543  
1544 2. If the pole is real and there are no other remaining real poles [#]_,
1545 add the closest real zero to the section and leave it as a first
1546 order section. Note that after this step we are guaranteed to be
1547 left with an even number of real poles, complex poles, real zeros,
1548 and complex zeros for subsequent pairing iterations.
1549  
1550 3. Else:
1551  
1552 1. If the pole is complex and the zero is the only remaining real
1553 zero*, then pair the pole with the *next* closest zero
1554 (guaranteed to be complex). This is necessary to ensure that
1555 there will be a real zero remaining to eventually create a
1556 first-order section (thus keeping the odd order).
1557  
1558 2. Else pair the pole with the closest remaining zero (complex or
1559 real).
1560  
1561 3. Proceed to complete the second-order section by adding another
1562 pole and zero to the current pole and zero in the section:
1563  
1564 1. If the current pole and zero are both complex, add their
1565 conjugates.
1566  
1567 2. Else if the pole is complex and the zero is real, add the
1568 conjugate pole and the next closest real zero.
1569  
1570 3. Else if the pole is real and the zero is complex, add the
1571 conjugate zero and the real pole closest to those zeros.
1572  
1573 4. Else (we must have a real pole and real zero) add the next
1574 real pole closest to the unit circle, and then add the real
1575 zero closest to that pole.
1576  
1577 .. [#] This conditional can only be met for specific odd-order inputs
1578 with the ``pairing = 'keep_odd'`` or ``'minimal'`` methods.
1579  
1580 .. versionadded:: 0.16.0
1581  
1582 Examples
1583 --------
1584  
1585 Design a 6th order low-pass elliptic digital filter for a system with a
1586 sampling rate of 8000 Hz that has a pass-band corner frequency of
1587 1000 Hz. The ripple in the pass-band should not exceed 0.087 dB, and
1588 the attenuation in the stop-band should be at least 90 dB.
1589  
1590 In the following call to `ellip`, we could use ``output='sos'``,
1591 but for this example, we'll use ``output='zpk'``, and then convert
1592 to SOS format with `zpk2sos`:
1593  
1594 >>> from scipy import signal
1595 >>> import numpy as np
1596 >>> z, p, k = signal.ellip(6, 0.087, 90, 1000/(0.5*8000), output='zpk')
1597  
1598 Now convert to SOS format.
1599  
1600 >>> sos = signal.zpk2sos(z, p, k)
1601  
1602 The coefficients of the numerators of the sections:
1603  
1604 >>> sos[:, :3]
1605 array([[0.0014152 , 0.00248677, 0.0014152 ],
1606 [1. , 0.72976874, 1. ],
1607 [1. , 0.17607852, 1. ]])
1608  
1609 The symmetry in the coefficients occurs because all the zeros are on the
1610 unit circle.
1611  
1612 The coefficients of the denominators of the sections:
1613  
1614 >>> sos[:, 3:]
1615 array([[ 1. , -1.32544025, 0.46989976],
1616 [ 1. , -1.26118294, 0.62625924],
1617 [ 1. , -1.2570723 , 0.8619958 ]])
1618  
1619 The next example shows the effect of the `pairing` option. We have a
1620 system with three poles and three zeros, so the SOS array will have
1621 shape (2, 6). The means there is, in effect, an extra pole and an extra
1622 zero at the origin in the SOS representation.
1623  
1624 >>> z1 = np.array([-1, -0.5-0.5j, -0.5+0.5j])
1625 >>> p1 = np.array([0.75, 0.8+0.1j, 0.8-0.1j])
1626  
1627 With ``pairing='nearest'`` (the default), we obtain
1628  
1629 >>> signal.zpk2sos(z1, p1, 1)
1630 array([[ 1. , 1. , 0.5 , 1. , -0.75, 0. ],
1631 [ 1. , 1. , 0. , 1. , -1.6 , 0.65]])
1632  
1633 The first section has the zeros {-0.5-0.05j, -0.5+0.5j} and the poles
1634 {0, 0.75}, and the second section has the zeros {-1, 0} and poles
1635 {0.8+0.1j, 0.8-0.1j}. Note that the extra pole and zero at the origin
1636 have been assigned to different sections.
1637  
1638 With ``pairing='keep_odd'``, we obtain:
1639  
1640 >>> signal.zpk2sos(z1, p1, 1, pairing='keep_odd')
1641 array([[ 1. , 1. , 0. , 1. , -0.75, 0. ],
1642 [ 1. , 1. , 0.5 , 1. , -1.6 , 0.65]])
1643  
1644 The extra pole and zero at the origin are in the same section.
1645 The first section is, in effect, a first-order section.
1646  
1647 With ``pairing='minimal'``, the first-order section doesn't have
1648 the extra pole and zero at the origin:
1649  
1650 >>> signal.zpk2sos(z1, p1, 1, pairing='minimal')
1651 array([[ 0. , 1. , 1. , 0. , 1. , -0.75],
1652 [ 1. , 1. , 0.5 , 1. , -1.6 , 0.65]])
1653  
1654 """
1655 # TODO in the near future:
1656 # 1. Add SOS capability to `filtfilt`, `freqz`, etc. somehow (#3259).
1657 # 2. Make `decimate` use `sosfilt` instead of `lfilter`.
1658 # 3. Make sosfilt automatically simplify sections to first order
1659 # when possible. Note this might make `sosfiltfilt` a bit harder (ICs).
1660 # 4. Further optimizations of the section ordering / pole-zero pairing.
1661 # See the wiki for other potential issues.
1662  
1663 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
1664  
1665 # convert to numpy, convert back on exit XXX
1666 z, p = map(np.asarray, (z, p))
1667 k = np.asarray(k)
1668  
1669 if pairing is None:
1670 pairing = 'minimal' if analog else 'nearest'
1671  
1672 valid_pairings = ['nearest', 'keep_odd', 'minimal']
1673 if pairing not in valid_pairings:
  • E501 Line too long (83 > 79 characters)
1674 raise ValueError(f'pairing must be one of {valid_pairings}, not {pairing}')
1675  
1676 if analog and pairing != 'minimal':
1677 raise ValueError('for analog zpk2sos conversion, '
1678 'pairing must be "minimal"')
1679  
1680 if len(z) == len(p) == 0:
1681 if not analog:
1682 return xp.asarray(np.asarray([[k, 0., 0., 1., 0., 0.]]))
1683 else:
1684 return xp.asarray(np.asarray([[0., 0., k, 0., 0., 1.]]))
1685

1798 def _align_nums(nums, xp):
1799 """Aligns the shapes of multiple numerators.
1800  
1801 Given an array of numerator coefficient arrays [[a_1, a_2,...,
1802 a_n],..., [b_1, b_2,..., b_m]], this function pads shorter numerator
1803 arrays with zero's so that all numerators have the same length. Such
1804 alignment is necessary for functions like 'tf2ss', which needs the
1805 alignment when dealing with SIMO transfer functions.
1806  
1807 Parameters
1808 ----------
1809 nums: array_like
1810 Numerator or list of numerators. Not necessarily with same length.
1811  
1812 Returns
1813 -------
1814 nums: array
1815 The numerator. If `nums` input was a list of numerators then a 2-D
1816 array with padded zeros for shorter numerators is returned. Otherwise
1817 returns ``np.asarray(nums)``.
1818 """
1819 try:
1820 # The statement can throw a ValueError if one
1821 # of the numerators is a single digit and another
1822 # is array-like e.g. if nums = [5, [1, 2, 3]]
1823 nums = xp.asarray(nums)
1824  
1825 if not xp.isdtype(nums.dtype, "numeric"):
1826 raise ValueError("dtype of numerator is non-numeric")
1827  
1828 return nums
1829  
1830 except ValueError:
1831 nums = [xpx.atleast_nd(xp.asarray(num), ndim=1) for num in nums]
1832 max_width = max(xp_size(num) for num in nums)
1833  
1834 # pre-allocate
1835 aligned_nums = xp.zeros((len(nums), max_width))
1836  
1837 # Create numerators with padded zeros
1838 for index, num in enumerate(nums):
1839 aligned_nums[index, -num.size:] = num
1840  
1841 return aligned_nums
1842  
1843  
1844 def normalize(b, a):
1845 """Normalize numerator/denominator of a continuous-time transfer function.
1846  
1847 If values of `b` are too close to 0, they are removed. In that case, a
1848 BadCoefficients warning is emitted.
1849  
1850 Parameters
1851 ----------
1852 b: array_like
1853 Numerator of the transfer function. Can be a 2-D array to normalize
1854 multiple transfer functions.
1855 a: array_like
1856 Denominator of the transfer function. At most 1-D.
1857  
1858 Returns
1859 -------
1860 num: array
1861 The numerator of the normalized transfer function. At least a 1-D
1862 array. A 2-D array if the input `num` is a 2-D array.
1863 den: 1-D array
1864 The denominator of the normalized transfer function.
1865  
1866 Notes
1867 -----
1868 Coefficients for both the numerator and denominator should be specified in
1869 descending exponent order (e.g., ``s^2 + 3s + 5`` would be represented as
1870 ``[1, 3, 5]``).
1871

1873 --------

2008 xp = array_namespace(a, b)
2009 a, b = map(xp.asarray, (a, b))
2010 a, b = xp_promote(a, b, force_floating=True, xp=xp)
2011 a = xpx.atleast_nd(a, ndim=1, xp=xp)
2012 b = xpx.atleast_nd(b, ndim=1, xp=xp)
2013  
2014 try:
2015 wo = float(wo)
2016 except TypeError:
2017 wo = float(wo[0])
2018 d = a.shape[0]
2019 n = b.shape[0]
2020 M = max((d, n))
2021 pwo = wo ** xp.arange(M - 1, -1, -1, dtype=xp.float64)
2022 start1 = max((n - d, 0))
2023 start2 = max((d - n, 0))
2024 b = b * pwo[start1] / pwo[start2:]
2025 a = a * pwo[start1] / pwo[start1:]

2029 def _resize(a, new_shape, xp):
2030 # https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.2.4/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py#L1535
2031 a = xp.reshape(a, (-1,))
2032  
2033 new_size = 1
2034 for dim_length in new_shape:
2035 new_size *= dim_length
2036 if dim_length < 0:
2037 raise ValueError(
2038 'all elements of `new_shape` must be non-negative'
2039 )
2040  
2041 if xp_size(a) == 0 or new_size == 0:
2042 # First case must zero fill. The second would have repeats == 0.
2043 return xp.zeros_like(a, shape=new_shape)
2044  
2045 repeats = -(-new_size // xp_size(a)) # ceil division
2046 a = xp.concat((a,) * repeats)[:new_size]
2047  
2048 return xp.reshape(a, new_shape)

2196 >>> plt.xlabel('Frequency [rad/s]')

2201  
2202 a, b = map(xp.asarray, (a, b))
2203 a, b = xp_promote(a, b, force_floating=True, xp=xp)
2204 a = xpx.atleast_nd(a, ndim=1, xp=xp)
2205 b = xpx.atleast_nd(b, ndim=1, xp=xp)
2206  
2207 D = a.shape[0] - 1
2208 N = b.shape[0] - 1
2209 ma = max([N, D])
2210 Np = N + ma
2211 Dp = D + ma
2212 bprime = xp.empty(Np + 1, dtype=b.dtype)
2213 aprime = xp.empty(Dp + 1, dtype=a.dtype)

2216 val = 0.0
2217 for i in range(0, N + 1):
2218 for k in range(0, i + 1):
2219 if ma - i + 2 * k == j:
2220 val += comb(i, k) * b[N - i] * (wosq) ** (i - k) / bw ** i
2221 bprime[Np - j] = val
2222 for j in range(Dp + 1):
2223 val = 0.0
2224 for i in range(0, D + 1):
2225 for k in range(0, i + 1):
2226 if ma - i + 2 * k == j:
2227 val += comb(i, k) * a[D - i] * (wosq) ** (i - k) / bw ** i
2228 aprime[Dp - j] = val
2229  
2230 return normalize(bprime, aprime)

2359  
2360 H_a(s) = \frac{b_0 s^Q + b_1 s^{Q-1} + \cdots + b_Q}{
2361 a_0 s^P + a_1 s^{P-1} + \cdots + a_P}\ .
2362  
2363 The bilinear transform [1]_ is applied by substituting
2364  
2365 .. math::
2366  
2367 s = \kappa \frac{z-1}{z+1}\ , \qquad \kappa := 2 f_s\ ,
2368  
2369 into :math:`H_a(s)`, with :math:`f_s` being the sampling rate.
2370 This results in the digital transfer function in the :math:`z`-domain
2371  
2372 .. math::
2373  
2374 H_d(z) = \frac{b_0 \left(\kappa \frac{z-1}{z+1}\right)^Q +
2375 b_1 \left(\kappa \frac{z-1}{z+1}\right)^{Q-1} +
2376 \cdots + b_Q}{
2377 a_0 \left(\kappa \frac{z-1}{z+1}\right)^P +
2378 a_1 \left(\kappa \frac{z-1}{z+1}\right)^{P-1} +
2379 \cdots + a_P}\ .
2380  
  • E501 Line too long (81 > 79 characters)
2381 This expression can be simplified by multiplying numerator and denominator by
  • E501 Line too long (80 > 79 characters)
2382 :math:`(z+1)^N`, with :math:`N=\max(P, Q)`. This allows :math:`H_d(z)` to be
2383 reformulated as

2386  
2387 & & \frac{b_0 \big(\kappa (z-1)\big)^Q (z+1)^{N-Q} +
2388 b_1 \big(\kappa (z-1)\big)^{Q-1} (z+1)^{N-Q+1} +
2389 \cdots + b_Q(z+1)^N}{
2390 a_0 \big(\kappa (z-1)\big)^P (z+1)^{N-P} +
2391 a_1 \big(\kappa (z-1)\big)^{P-1} (z+1)^{N-P+1} +
2392 \cdots + a_P(z+1)^N}\\
2393 &=:& \frac{\beta_0 + \beta_1 z^{-1} + \cdots + \beta_N z^{-N}}{

2651 def iirfilter(N, Wn, rp=None, rs=None, btype='band', analog=False,
2652 ftype='butter', output='ba', fs=None):
2653 """
2654 IIR digital and analog filter design given order and critical points.
2655  
2656 Design an Nth-order digital or analog filter and return the filter
2657 coefficients.
2658  
2659 Parameters
2660 ----------
2661 N : int
2662 The order of the filter.
2663 Wn : array_like
2664 A scalar or length-2 sequence giving the critical frequencies.
2665  
2666 For digital filters, `Wn` are in the same units as `fs`. By default,
2667 `fs` is 2 half-cycles/sample, so these are normalized from 0 to 1,
2668 where 1 is the Nyquist frequency. (`Wn` is thus in
2669 half-cycles / sample.)
2670  
2671 For analog filters, `Wn` is an angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
2672  
2673 When Wn is a length-2 sequence, ``Wn[0]`` must be less than ``Wn[1]``.
2674 rp : float, optional
2675 For Chebyshev and elliptic filters, provides the maximum ripple
2676 in the passband. (dB)
2677 rs : float, optional
2678 For Chebyshev and elliptic filters, provides the minimum attenuation
2679 in the stop band. (dB)
2680 btype : {'bandpass', 'lowpass', 'highpass', 'bandstop'}, optional
2681 The type of filter. Default is 'bandpass'.
2682 analog : bool, optional
2683 When True, return an analog filter, otherwise a digital filter is
2684 returned.
2685 ftype : str, optional
2686 The type of IIR filter to design:
2687  
2688 - Butterworth : 'butter'
2689 - Chebyshev I : 'cheby1'
2690 - Chebyshev II : 'cheby2'
2691 - Cauer/elliptic: 'ellip'
2692 - Bessel/Thomson: 'bessel'
2693  
2694 output : {'ba', 'zpk', 'sos'}, optional
2695 Filter form of the output:
2696  
2697 - second-order sections (recommended): 'sos'
2698 - numerator/denominator (default) : 'ba'
2699 - pole-zero : 'zpk'
2700  
2701 In general the second-order sections ('sos') form is
2702 recommended because inferring the coefficients for the
2703 numerator/denominator form ('ba') suffers from numerical
2704 instabilities. For reasons of backward compatibility the default
2705 form is the numerator/denominator form ('ba'), where the 'b'
2706 and the 'a' in 'ba' refer to the commonly used names of the
2707 coefficients used.
2708  
2709 Note: Using the second-order sections form ('sos') is sometimes
2710 associated with additional computational costs: for
2711 data-intense use cases it is therefore recommended to also
2712 investigate the numerator/denominator form ('ba').
2713  
2714 fs : float, optional
2715 The sampling frequency of the digital system.
2716  
2717 .. versionadded:: 1.2.0
2718  
2719 Returns
2720 -------
2721 b, a : ndarray, ndarray
2722 Numerator (`b`) and denominator (`a`) polynomials of the IIR filter.
2723 Only returned if ``output='ba'``.
2724 z, p, k : ndarray, ndarray, float
2725 Zeros, poles, and system gain of the IIR filter transfer
2726 function. Only returned if ``output='zpk'``.
2727 sos : ndarray
2728 Second-order sections representation of the IIR filter.
2729 Only returned if ``output='sos'``.
2730  
2731 See Also
2732 --------
2733 butter : Filter design using order and critical points
2734 cheby1, cheby2, ellip, bessel

2736 cheb1ord, cheb2ord, ellipord

2743 Examples
2744 --------
2745 Generate a 17th-order Chebyshev II analog bandpass filter from 50 Hz to
2746 200 Hz and plot the frequency response:
2747  
2748 >>> import numpy as np
2749 >>> from scipy import signal
2750 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

2752 >>> b, a = signal.iirfilter(17, [2*np.pi*50, 2*np.pi*200], rs=60,
2753 ... btype='band', analog=True, ftype='cheby2')

2755 >>> fig = plt.figure()
2756 >>> ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 1, 1)
2757 >>> ax.semilogx(w / (2*np.pi), 20 * np.log10(np.maximum(abs(h), 1e-5)))

2759 >>> ax.set_xlabel('Frequency [Hz]')

2761 >>> ax.axis((10, 1000, -100, 10))

2766 sampling rate of 2000 Hz, and plot the frequency response. (Second-order
2767 sections implementation is required to ensure stability of a filter of
2768 this order):
2769  
2770 >>> sos = signal.iirfilter(17, [50, 200], rs=60, btype='band',
2771 ... analog=False, ftype='cheby2', fs=2000,

2773 >>> w, h = signal.freqz_sos(sos, 2000, fs=2000)
2774 >>> fig = plt.figure()

2780 >>> ax.axis((10, 1000, -100, 10))
2781 >>> ax.grid(which='both', axis='both')
2782 >>> plt.show()

2787 Wn = asarray(Wn)

2892 def _relative_degree(z, p):
2893 """
2894 Return relative degree of transfer function from zeros and poles
2895 """
2896 degree = p.shape[0] - z.shape[0]
2897 if degree < 0:
2898 raise ValueError("Improper transfer function. "
2899 "Must have at least as many poles as zeros.")
2900 else:
2901 return degree

2904 def bilinear_zpk(z, p, k, fs):
2905 r"""
2906 Return a digital IIR filter from an analog one using a bilinear transform.
2907  
2908 Transform a set of poles and zeros from the analog s-plane to the digital
2909 z-plane using Tustin's method, which substitutes ``2*fs*(z-1) / (z+1)`` for
2910 ``s``, maintaining the shape of the frequency response.
2911  
2912 Parameters
2913 ----------
2914 z : array_like
2915 Zeros of the analog filter transfer function.
2916 p : array_like
2917 Poles of the analog filter transfer function.
2918 k : float
2919 System gain of the analog filter transfer function.
2920 fs : float
2921 Sample rate, as ordinary frequency (e.g., hertz). No prewarping is
2922 done in this function.
2923  
2924 Returns
2925 -------
2926 z : ndarray
2927 Zeros of the transformed digital filter transfer function.
2928 p : ndarray
2929 Poles of the transformed digital filter transfer function.
2930 k : float
2931 System gain of the transformed digital filter.
2932  
2933 See Also
2934 --------
2935 lp2lp_zpk, lp2hp_zpk, lp2bp_zpk, lp2bs_zpk
2936 bilinear
2937  
2938 Notes
2939 -----
2940 .. versionadded:: 1.1.0
2941  
2942 Examples
2943 --------
2944 >>> import numpy as np
2945 >>> from scipy import signal
2946 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
2947  
2948 >>> fs = 100
2949 >>> bf = 2 * np.pi * np.array([7, 13])
2950 >>> filts = signal.lti(*signal.butter(4, bf, btype='bandpass', analog=True,
2951 ... output='zpk'))
2952 >>> filtz = signal.lti(*signal.bilinear_zpk(filts.zeros, filts.poles,
2953 ... filts.gain, fs))
2954 >>> wz, hz = signal.freqz_zpk(filtz.zeros, filtz.poles, filtz.gain)
2955 >>> ws, hs = signal.freqs_zpk(filts.zeros, filts.poles, filts.gain,
2956 ... worN=fs*wz)
2957 >>> plt.semilogx(wz*fs/(2*np.pi), 20*np.log10(np.abs(hz).clip(1e-15)),
2958 ... label=r'$|H_z(e^{j \omega})|$')
2959 >>> plt.semilogx(wz*fs/(2*np.pi), 20*np.log10(np.abs(hs).clip(1e-15)),
2960 ... label=r'$|H(j \omega)|$')
2961 >>> plt.legend()
2962 >>> plt.xlabel('Frequency [Hz]')
2963 >>> plt.ylabel('Amplitude [dB]')
2964 >>> plt.grid(True)
2965 """
2966 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
2967  
2968 z, p = map(xp.asarray, (z, p))
2969 z = xpx.atleast_nd(z, ndim=1, xp=xp)
2970 p = xpx.atleast_nd(p, ndim=1, xp=xp)
2971  
2972 fs = _validate_fs(fs, allow_none=False)
2973  
2974 degree = _relative_degree(z, p)
2975  
2976 fs2 = 2.0*fs
2977  
2978 # Bilinear transform the poles and zeros
2979 z_z = (fs2 + z) / (fs2 - z)
2980 p_z = (fs2 + p) / (fs2 - p)
2981  
2982 # Any zeros that were at infinity get moved to the Nyquist frequency
2983 z_z = xp.concat((z_z, -xp.ones(degree)))
2984  
2985 # Compensate for gain change
2986 k_z = k * xp.real(xp.prod(fs2 - z) / xp.prod(fs2 - p))
2987  
2988 return z_z, p_z, k_z
2989

2992 r"""
2993 Transform a lowpass filter prototype to a different frequency.
2994

2996 from an analog low-pass filter prototype with unity cutoff frequency,
2997 using zeros, poles, and gain ('zpk') representation.

3000 ----------

3006 System gain of the analog filter transfer function.
3007 wo : float
3008 Desired cutoff, as angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
3009 Defaults to no change.
3010

3012 -------
3013 z : ndarray
3014 Zeros of the transformed low-pass filter transfer function.
3015 p : ndarray

3029 .. math:: s \rightarrow \frac{s}{\omega_0}

3031 .. versionadded:: 1.1.0

3033 Examples

3035 Use the 'zpk' (Zero-Pole-Gain) representation of a lowpass filter to

3045 """
3046 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
3047  
3048 z, p = map(xp.asarray, (z, p))
3049 z = xpx.atleast_nd(z, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3050 p = xpx.atleast_nd(p, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3051  
3052 wo = float(wo) # Avoid int wraparound
3053  
3054 degree = _relative_degree(z, p)
3055  
3056 # Scale all points radially from origin to shift cutoff frequency
3057 z_lp = wo * z
3058 p_lp = wo * p
3059  
3060 # Each shifted pole decreases gain by wo, each shifted zero increases it.
3061 # Cancel out the net change to keep overall gain the same
3062 k_lp = k * wo**degree
3063  
3064 return z_lp, p_lp, k_lp
3065  
3066  
3067 def lp2hp_zpk(z, p, k, wo=1.0):
3068 r"""
3069 Transform a lowpass filter prototype to a highpass filter.
3070  
3071 Return an analog high-pass filter with cutoff frequency `wo`
3072 from an analog low-pass filter prototype with unity cutoff frequency,
3073 using zeros, poles, and gain ('zpk') representation.
3074  
3075 Parameters
3076 ----------
3077 z : array_like
3078 Zeros of the analog filter transfer function.
3079 p : array_like
3080 Poles of the analog filter transfer function.
3081 k : float
3082 System gain of the analog filter transfer function.
3083 wo : float
3084 Desired cutoff, as angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
3085 Defaults to no change.
3086  
3087 Returns
3088 -------
3089 z : ndarray
3090 Zeros of the transformed high-pass filter transfer function.
3091 p : ndarray
3092 Poles of the transformed high-pass filter transfer function.
3093 k : float
3094 System gain of the transformed high-pass filter.
3095  
3096 See Also
3097 --------
3098 lp2lp_zpk, lp2bp_zpk, lp2bs_zpk, bilinear
3099 lp2hp
3100  
3101 Notes
3102 -----
3103 This is derived from the s-plane substitution
3104  
3105 .. math:: s \rightarrow \frac{\omega_0}{s}
3106  
3107 This maintains symmetry of the lowpass and highpass responses on a
3108 logarithmic scale.
3109  
3110 .. versionadded:: 1.1.0
3111  
3112 Examples
3113 --------
3114 Use the 'zpk' (Zero-Pole-Gain) representation of a lowpass filter to
3115 transform it to a highpass filter with a cutoff frequency wo.
3116  
3117 >>> from scipy.signal import lp2hp_zpk
3118 >>> z = [ -2 + 3j , -0.5 - 0.8j ]
3119 >>> p = [ -1 , -4 ]
3120 >>> k = 10
3121 >>> wo = 0.6
3122 >>> lp2hp_zpk(z, p, k, wo)
3123 ( array([-0.09230769-0.13846154j, -0.33707865+0.53932584j]),
3124 array([-0.6 , -0.15]),
3125 8.5)
3126 """
3127 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
3128  
3129 z, p = map(xp.asarray, (z, p))
3130 # XXX: no xp_promote here since that breaks TestButter
3131 z = xpx.atleast_nd(z, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3132 p = xpx.atleast_nd(p, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3133  
3134 wo = float(wo)
3135  
3136 degree = _relative_degree(z, p)
3137  
3138 # Invert positions radially about unit circle to convert LPF to HPF
3139 # Scale all points radially from origin to shift cutoff frequency
3140 z_hp = wo / z
3141 p_hp = wo / p
3142  
3143 # If lowpass had zeros at infinity, inverting moves them to origin.
3144 z_hp = xp.concat((z_hp, xp.zeros(degree)))
3145  
3146 # Cancel out gain change caused by inversion
3147 k_hp = k * xp.real(xp.prod(-z) / xp.prod(-p))
3148  
3149 return z_hp, p_hp, k_hp
3150  
3151  
3152 def lp2bp_zpk(z, p, k, wo=1.0, bw=1.0):
3153 r"""
3154 Transform a lowpass filter prototype to a bandpass filter.
3155  
3156 Return an analog band-pass filter with center frequency `wo` and
3157 bandwidth `bw` from an analog low-pass filter prototype with unity
3158 cutoff frequency, using zeros, poles, and gain ('zpk') representation.
3159  
3160 Parameters
3161 ----------
3162 z : array_like
3163 Zeros of the analog filter transfer function.
3164 p : array_like
3165 Poles of the analog filter transfer function.
3166 k : float
3167 System gain of the analog filter transfer function.
3168 wo : float
3169 Desired passband center, as angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
3170 Defaults to no change.
3171 bw : float
3172 Desired passband width, as angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
3173 Defaults to 1.
3174  
3175 Returns
3176 -------
3177 z : ndarray
3178 Zeros of the transformed band-pass filter transfer function.
3179 p : ndarray
3180 Poles of the transformed band-pass filter transfer function.
3181 k : float
3182 System gain of the transformed band-pass filter.
3183  
3184 See Also
3185 --------
3186 lp2lp_zpk, lp2hp_zpk, lp2bs_zpk, bilinear
3187 lp2bp
3188  
3189 Notes
3190 -----
3191 This is derived from the s-plane substitution
3192  
3193 .. math:: s \rightarrow \frac{s^2 + {\omega_0}^2}{s \cdot \mathrm{BW}}
3194  
3195 This is the "wideband" transformation, producing a passband with
3196 geometric (log frequency) symmetry about `wo`.
3197  
3198 .. versionadded:: 1.1.0
3199  
3200 Examples
3201 --------
3202 Use the 'zpk' (Zero-Pole-Gain) representation of a lowpass filter to
3203 transform it to a bandpass filter with a center frequency wo and
3204 bandwidth bw.
3205  
3206 >>> from scipy.signal import lp2bp_zpk
3207 >>> z = [ 5 + 2j , 5 - 2j ]
3208 >>> p = [ 7 , -16 ]
3209 >>> k = 0.8
3210 >>> wo = 0.62
3211 >>> bw = 15
3212 >>> lp2bp_zpk(z, p, k, wo, bw)
3213 ( array([7.49955815e+01+3.00017676e+01j, 7.49955815e+01-3.00017676e+01j,
  • E501 Line too long (80 > 79 characters)
3214 4.41850748e-03-1.76761126e-03j, 4.41850748e-03+1.76761126e-03j]),
3215 array([1.04996339e+02+0.j, -1.60167736e-03+0.j, 3.66108003e-03+0.j,
3216 -2.39998398e+02+0.j]), 0.8)
3217 """
3218 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
3219  
3220 z, p = map(xp.asarray, (z, p))
3221 z, p = xp_promote(z, p, force_floating=True, xp=xp)
3222 z = xpx.atleast_nd(z, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3223 p = xpx.atleast_nd(p, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3224  
3225 wo = float(wo)
3226 bw = float(bw)
3227  
3228 degree = _relative_degree(z, p)
3229  
3230 # Scale poles and zeros to desired bandwidth
3231 z_lp = z * bw/2
3232 p_lp = p * bw/2
3233  
3234 # Square root needs to produce complex result, not NaN
3235 z_lp = xp.astype(z_lp, xp.complex128)
3236 p_lp = xp.astype(p_lp, xp.complex128)
3237  
3238 # Duplicate poles and zeros and shift from baseband to +wo and -wo
3239 z_bp = xp.concat((z_lp + xp.sqrt(z_lp**2 - wo**2),
3240 z_lp - xp.sqrt(z_lp**2 - wo**2)))
3241 p_bp = xp.concat((p_lp + xp.sqrt(p_lp**2 - wo**2),
3242 p_lp - xp.sqrt(p_lp**2 - wo**2)))
3243  
3244 # Move degree zeros to origin, leaving degree zeros at infinity for BPF
3245 z_bp = xp.concat((z_bp, xp.zeros(degree)))
3246  
3247 # Cancel out gain change from frequency scaling
3248 k_bp = k * bw**degree
3249  
3250 return z_bp, p_bp, k_bp
3251  
3252  
3253 def lp2bs_zpk(z, p, k, wo=1.0, bw=1.0):
3254 r"""
3255 Transform a lowpass filter prototype to a bandstop filter.
3256  
3257 Return an analog band-stop filter with center frequency `wo` and
3258 stopband width `bw` from an analog low-pass filter prototype with unity
3259 cutoff frequency, using zeros, poles, and gain ('zpk') representation.
3260  
3261 Parameters
3262 ----------
3263 z : array_like
3264 Zeros of the analog filter transfer function.
3265 p : array_like
3266 Poles of the analog filter transfer function.
3267 k : float
3268 System gain of the analog filter transfer function.
3269 wo : float
3270 Desired stopband center, as angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
3271 Defaults to no change.
3272 bw : float
3273 Desired stopband width, as angular frequency (e.g., rad/s).
3274 Defaults to 1.
3275  
3276 Returns
3277 -------
3278 z : ndarray
3279 Zeros of the transformed band-stop filter transfer function.
3280 p : ndarray
3281 Poles of the transformed band-stop filter transfer function.
3282 k : float
3283 System gain of the transformed band-stop filter.
3284  
3285 See Also
3286 --------
3287 lp2lp_zpk, lp2hp_zpk, lp2bp_zpk, bilinear
3288 lp2bs
3289  
3290 Notes
3291 -----
3292 This is derived from the s-plane substitution
3293  
3294 .. math:: s \rightarrow \frac{s \cdot \mathrm{BW}}{s^2 + {\omega_0}^2}
3295  
3296 This is the "wideband" transformation, producing a stopband with
3297 geometric (log frequency) symmetry about `wo`.
3298  
3299 .. versionadded:: 1.1.0
3300  
3301 Examples
3302 --------
3303 Transform a low-pass filter represented in 'zpk' (Zero-Pole-Gain) form
  • E501 Line too long (84 > 79 characters)
3304 into a bandstop filter represented in 'zpk' form, with a center frequency wo and
3305 bandwidth bw.
3306  
3307 >>> from scipy.signal import lp2bs_zpk
3308 >>> z = [ ]
3309 >>> p = [ 0.7 , -1 ]
3310 >>> k = 9
3311 >>> wo = 0.5
3312 >>> bw = 10
3313 >>> lp2bs_zpk(z, p, k, wo, bw)
3314 ( array([0.+0.5j, 0.+0.5j, 0.-0.5j, 0.-0.5j]),
  • E501 Line too long (84 > 79 characters)
3315 array([14.2681928 +0.j, -0.02506281+0.j, 0.01752149+0.j, -9.97493719+0.j]),
3316 -12.857142857142858)
3317 """
3318 xp = array_namespace(z, p)
3319  
3320 z, p = map(xp.asarray, (z, p))
3321 z, p = xp_promote(z, p, force_floating=True, xp=xp)
3322 z = xpx.atleast_nd(z, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3323 p = xpx.atleast_nd(p, ndim=1, xp=xp)
3324  
3325 wo = float(wo)
3326 bw = float(bw)
3327  
3328 degree = _relative_degree(z, p)
3329  
3330 # Invert to a highpass filter with desired bandwidth
3331 z_hp = (bw/2) / z
3332 p_hp = (bw/2) / p
3333  
3334 # Square root needs to produce complex result, not NaN
3335 z_hp = xp.astype(z_hp, xp.complex128)
3336 p_hp = xp.astype(p_hp, xp.complex128)
3337  
3338 # Duplicate poles and zeros and shift from baseband to +wo and -wo
3339 z_bs = xp.concat((z_hp + xp.sqrt(z_hp**2 - wo**2),
3340 z_hp - xp.sqrt(z_hp**2 - wo**2)))
3341 p_bs = xp.concat((p_hp + xp.sqrt(p_hp**2 - wo**2),
3342 p_hp - xp.sqrt(p_hp**2 - wo**2)))
3343  
3344 # Move any zeros that were at infinity to the center of the stopband
3345 z_bs = xp.concat((z_bs, xp.full(degree, +1j*wo)))
3346 z_bs = xp.concat((z_bs, xp.full(degree, -1j*wo)))
3347  
3348 # Cancel out gain change caused by inversion
3349 k_bs = k * xp.real(xp.prod(-z) / xp.prod(-p))
3350  
3351 return z_bs, p_bs, k_bs
